question: What is your main responsibility as a midwife when giving any drug to a patient?

options.B: Ordering new stock from the pharmacy

explanation: As the midwife administering the medication at that moment, patient safety is your ultimate responsibility. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T1#BMP120_U2_T1_h1)

question: Why should you keep a questioning attitude instead of blindly giving a charted drug?

options.A: To make doctors rewrite their treatment plans
options.B: To test the knowledge of the pharmacy staff
options.C: To delay the hospital discharge process
options.D: To prevent avoidable harm from medication errors

explanation: Drugs are powerful agents, and questioning unusual orders helps catch mistakes before they hurt the patient. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T1#BMP120_U2_T1_h1)

question: Which practice helps prevent germs from contaminating an injection?

options.D: Warming the drug in warm water

explanation: Aseptic technique ensures that harmful germs do not enter the patient's body during drug preparation and delivery. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T1#BMP120_U2_T1_h2)

question: You check the prescribed time for an antibiotic dose to keep steady blood levels. Which core principle is this?
explanation: Administering drugs within the correct time window ensures the medication stays at a therapeutic level in the body. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T1#BMP120_U2_T1_h2)

question: How many times should you check the drug label against the prescription sheet?
explanation: Checking the drug label three times reduces the chance of missing a discrepancy before administration. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T1#BMP120_U2_T1_h3)

question: What does the 'Right Documentation' principle involve?

options.A: Recording the medication immediately after giving it
options.B: Writing down expected drug orders the night before
options.C: Leaving all charting until the end of the shift
options.D: Signing off drug charts before fetching the drugs

explanation: Documentation must happen right after administration to prevent accidental double-dosing or missed entries. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T1#BMP120_U2_T1_h3)

question: What is the safest way to verify a patient's identity before giving a medication?

options.A: Asking another patient in the ward to identify her
options.B: Calling out the surname and waiting for someone to nod
options.C: Looking at the bed number written on the chart
options.D: Checking the ID band and asking them to state their name

explanation: Using unique identifiers like the ID band and verbal confirmation prevents giving drugs to the wrong person. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T1#BMP120_U2_T1_h4)

question: You measure a pregnant woman's blood pressure before giving a prescribed antihypertensive drug. What is this action called?
explanation: Checking baseline parameters like blood pressure before giving a drug ensures it is safe to proceed with that dose. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T1#BMP120_U2_T1_h4)

question: Which of these is NOT a common contributing factor to medication errors in busy wards?
explanation: Sufficient and rested staff members actually reduce errors, whereas fatigue and shortages increase the risk of mistakes. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T1#BMP120_U2_T1_h5)

question: Why are verbal drug orders generally discouraged in routine clinical practice?

options.A: They take too long to write down later
options.B: They are easily misheard or misunderstood
options.C: Pharmacy departments refuse to supply them
options.D: They are illegal in all African countries

explanation: Spoken instructions lack a written paper trail and can be easily distorted in a noisy, busy clinical environment. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T1#BMP120_U2_T1_h5)

question: When must you sign the drug chart after administering a medication?

options.B: Whenever time permits the next day
options.C: At the end of the working shift

explanation: Charting must happen right after giving the drug to maintain an accurate, truthful record of care. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T1#BMP120_U2_T1_h6)

question: What is the proper professional response if you accidentally make a medication error?

options.A: Keep quiet so nobody else finds out about the mistake
options.B: Blame the junior student nurse who was standing nearby
options.C: Report it immediately and take steps to protect the patient
options.D: Cross out the entry and pretend nothing happened at all

explanation: Immediate disclosure allows the medical team to monitor the patient and manage any adverse effects safely. [learn more](BMP120_U2_T1#BMP120_U2_T1_h6)
